title: What is not allowed
html:
Each entry names the error, the rule it breaks and where that rule lives, and a failing instance whose conclusion is marked true or false: a wrong argument can reach either.

  1. Verifying instances and concluding “for all”. Breaks ∀I, which needs one proof about a fresh name (@def-rules-universal, Section 5.4). Instance: n2−n+11 is prime for n=0,1,…,10 (the values are 11,11,13,17,23,31,41,53,67,83,101), “so it is prime for every n∈N”. False: at n=11 the value is 121=112.
  2. A witness that depends on a variable introduced later, while uniformity is claimed. Breaks the side conditions of ∃E and ∀I: a witness δ0 obtained inside the box of x0 may not leave it (Section 6.4, @exm-converse-fails). Instance: “x2 is continuous at every x, with δ=min{1,ε/(2|x|+1)}; so one δ for each ε serves every x, and x2 is uniformly continuous on R”. False (@exm-square-not-uniform).
  3. Treating the name from ∃E as arbitrary. Breaks the side condition of ∀I: the witness appears in the open assumption of its box (@def-rules-existential, Section 5.6). Instance: “Some element of A is positive; let x be such an element. Since x was arbitrary, every element of A is positive.” False for A={−1,1}.
  4. Reusing one witness name for two ∃E’s. Breaks the fresh-name condition: the second name may not appear in an open assumption, and the first box’s assumption mentions it (Section 5.6, @exm-sum-of-evens). Sibling boxes may share a name. Instance: “m and n are even, so m=2k and n=2k for an integer k; hence m=n”. False: m=2, n=4.
  5. Proving the converse. Breaks →I, whose box opens with the hypothesis, not the conclusion (@def-rules-implication, Section 1.4). Instance: “If x2>1, then x>1: suppose x>1; then x2>x>1.” False: x=−2. Argument B of Section 1.1 makes the same move with a true conclusion.
  6. Affirming the consequent; denying the antecedent. Breaks @def-derivation (Section 1.4), being no rule: P→Q with Q gives no P, and with ¬P gives no ¬Q. Each pattern has a refuting row, so no derivation exists (@cor-refuting-row, Section 4.7): @exm-affirming-the-consequent, and for denying the row P false, Q true. Instances: “a multiple of 4 is even and 6 is even, so 6 is a multiple of 4”; “… and 6 is not a multiple of 4, so 6 is not even”. Both false.
  7. A missing case. Breaks ∨E, which needs one box for each disjunct (@def-rules-disjunction, Section 1.6). Instance: “|x|>0 for every real x: every real x has x>0, x=0 or x<0; if x>0, |x|=x>0; if x<0, |x|=−x>0”. False: the case x=0 was dropped, and |0|=0.
  8. Cases that do not exhaust. Breaks ∨E, whose first input must be a disjunction already derived (Section 1.6). Instance: “x2≥x for every real x: either x≥1 or x≤0; in the first case x2=x⋅x≥x, in the second x2≥0≥x”. False: x=1/2 satisfies neither case, and 1/4<1/2.
  9. Citing a line that is not available: the goal itself (circular reasoning), a result proved later, or a general “fact” neither proved nor a true school fact (a false “fact” never qualifies). Breaks @def-derivation: every line is a premise, an assumption, or a rule applied to available lines (Section 1.4). Instances: “if n2 is even, then n is even: suppose n2 is even; since n is even, …” (true, and circular); “x<1, so x2<1, since squaring preserves <” (false: x=−2).
  10. Using an assumption after its box has closed. Breaks the scope rule of @def-derivation (Section 1.4). Instance: “Suppose n is even, say n=2k; then n2=4k2. Hence if n is even, 4∣n2. Now n2=4k2, so 4∣n2 for every integer n.” False: n=1. Proof D below makes the same move with a true conclusion.
  11. A wrong negation, in three forms. Each breaks RAA, which closes only a box opened with ¬φ (Section 2.5), or the laws of Section 6.2.
      1. An RAA box opened with a statement that is not the negation of the goal. Instance: “if x2>9 and x>0, then x>3: suppose, for a contradiction, that x<3; then 0<x<3 gives x2<9, against x2>9; hence x>3” (true: the box should open with x≤3, and the case x=3 is never examined).
      1. A bound negated instead of a quantifier (@prp-bounded-quantifier-negation). Instance: “an=0 does not converge to 0, since some ε≤0 has |an−0|≥ε for all n” (false).
      1. The negation of φ→ψ written as an implication, ¬φ→¬ψ or φ→¬ψ, instead of φ∧¬ψ (@prp-negated-implication). Instance: “if x>2, then x2>4” is “refuted” because “if x≤2, then x2≤4” holds at x=0 (false: both are true at x=0, so one is not the negation of the other).
  12. Distinct letters taken for distinct objects. Two names introduced separately are treated as naming different objects, though no line says they differ. Breaks ∀I: a box opened for two arbitrary names must cover every pair, including the pairs in which both name one object (∀E may put the same term for both, @def-rule-universal-elimination). Instance: “if a and b are roots of x2−5x+6=0, then a+b=5: the two roots give x2−5x+6=(x−a)(x−b), and comparing coefficients, a+b=5”. False: a=b=2 are roots, and 2+2=4.
  13. An “and so on” with nothing behind it. A step is repeated “and so on”, and its outcome is used for every stage, but the passage from each stage to the next, or the reason the process ends, is never proved. Breaks @ax-induction (or @thm-strong-induction): →E on the axiom needs its step as a line, and “and so on” is not that line. Instance: “a non-empty set A of positive rational numbers has a least element: take a1∈A; if it is not least, take a2∈A with a2<a1, and so on, until the least element is reached” (false: {1/n:n∈Z>0} has no least element, and the process never ends).
  14. An object named before it is shown to exist. A step names an object, with “the …” or “let … be the …”, and so presupposes that such an object exists (for “the”, exactly one), though no line states or proves it. In (N9) the step asserts a fact that is not available; here the missing premise is never asserted at all, because it hides inside a name. Breaks ∃E, which opens its box only by citing a line ∃xφ (@def-rules-existential), and the use of “the” (Section 5.8), which needs existence and uniqueness. Instance: “let N be the largest natural number; then N+1≤N, so 1≤0” (false: the presupposed premise, that a largest natural number exists, is false).
